Q8031.L1t: Medical ethics rests on the principles of autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice, which can conflict in clinical practice.
Q8031.L2t: Physicians generally must keep patient information confidential, but this duty can yield when a identifiable third party faces serious, preventable harm.
Q8031.L3t: The wife has been exposed through unprotected sexual contact and may be infected without knowing it, so the physician's concern is preventing direct harm to her, which is the duty to avoid harming others.
Q8031.L4t: The physician's reason is that the duty to avoid harming the wife outweighs the patient's right to decide to keep his diagnosis secret.
Q8031.L2f: Medical ethics treats confidentiality as an absolute duty that applies equally to all diagnoses, with no recognized exceptions.
Q8031.L3f: The physician's recommendation is mainly about distributing scarce health resources fairly between the patient and his wife, so fairness is the principle that is being weighed against the patient's choice.
Q8031.L4f: The physician's reasoning is that the principle of justice outweighs the patient's autonomy in this case.

Q5772.L1t: The WHO's Global School-based Student Health Survey collects data on health behaviours and risk factors among students aged 13-15 in many countries.
Q5772.L2t: Physical fighting is one of the violence indicators measured in the survey, alongside bullying and physical attacks.
Q5772.L3t: The survey found that roughly one in five Chinese students aged 13-15 had been in a physical fight at school in the past year, which is well below a third.
Q5772.L4t: About 19 percent of Chinese children aged 13-15 reported being in a physical fight at school in the past 12 months as of 2015.
Q5772.L2f: The survey found that fighting was far rarer among Chinese students than in most other countries, and that fewer than one in twenty students took part.
Q5772.L3f: The survey found that a majority of Chinese students aged 13-15, a little under two in three, had been in a physical fight at school in the past year.
Q5772.L4f: About 59 percent of Chinese children aged 13-15 reported being in a physical fight at school in the past 12 months as of 2015.

Q8346.L1t: The Mughal Empire ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century and governed through local intermediaries such as zamindars.
Q8346.L2t: Akbar's administration relied on zamindars to collect land revenue and incorporated Rajput chiefs into the imperial structure.
Q8346.L3t: Akbar allowed Hindu and other non-Muslim local elites to keep their lands, faiths and authority within the empire, which left chiefs with the local base from which to claim independence.
Q8346.L4t: Zamindars could claim sovereignty largely because the Mughal Empire tolerated different religions and the local elites who practised them.
Q8346.L2f: Zamindars were salaried officials who were appointed by the emperor and moved between districts, so they held no hereditary local power.
Q8346.L3f: The Mughal state held that all subjects, including zamindars, were to be governed through an elected assembly with a broad right to vote, which gave local chiefs a political voice and a route to claim sovereignty.
Q8346.L4f: Zamindars could claim sovereignty largely because the Mughal Empire's policy gave the right to vote to its subjects.
